title: Day and night (1 Clement 24)
hookLine: Clement sees the resurrection in night turning to day and seed turning to plant
tomorrow: what does an anvil do while the hammer keeps coming down?

lines: DAY AND NIGHT SHOW A RESURRECTION.
WHY POINT AT SOMETHING SO ORDINARY?
cards: A weather app lists sunrise and sunset down to the minute, every single day, and almost nobody reads that line. An old letter sent from the church in Rome to the church in Corinth reads it like a sermon.
Day and night, it says, show us a resurrection. That's an odd thing to say. A sunrise isn't a miracle.
It happens every morning, whether anyone watches or not. So why point there?

teach.h: A LETTER FROM ROME TO CORINTH.
teach.b: The letter doesn't name its writer. Tradition gives it to Clement, a leader in the church at Rome.
In chapter twenty-four he asks the Corinthians to see how the Master keeps showing them the resurrection to come, with the Lord Jesus raised as its firstfruits. Then he points outside.
The night falls asleep, and the day rises. The day goes away, and the night comes on. Then he walks into a field.
A sower throws seed into the ground. It falls dry and bare, and it decays.
And out of that decay the Master's care raises it, and from one seed many grow and bear fruit.
So here's the answer to the puzzle: the ordinariness is the point. A picture that comes back every morning is a sermon nobody can miss. And the Corinthians had heard these pictures before.
Paul had written to that same church: "now is Christ risen from the dead, and become the firstfruits of them that slept."
And in John, Jesus says: "Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." Clement doesn't offer a proof.
He points at a sunrise and a field and says: look, something like it is already happening, small, every day.

how: Some churches hold Easter services at sunrise, and many Christians link the turning of day and night and the seasons with the hope of resurrection, as Clement does.

games.q: your little brother planted bean seeds in a cup. one has gone dry and shriveled, and he asks if it's ruined. what picture does 1 Clement 24 use?
o: a dry seed decays, and from it many grow.
a dead seed is gone for good.
only perfect seeds ever come up.
games.why: Clement's sower throws seed that falls dry and bare and decays, and from that decay many grow and bear fruit: a small picture of resurrection.

practice: Turn toward the nearest window, or bring to mind the last sky you saw. Watch the light as it is right now, and notice that it's moving, even if slowly. Let that slow change be the whole practice.

wordCard.voice: Day and night. Clement's first picture of resurrection: the night falls asleep, and the day rises.
